prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of the gains from trade and the empirical study of firms in international markets

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged from round 1. Melitz (2003) moved trade analysis from industries and representative firms to heterogeneous firms. Selection into exporting and reallocation across firms became a channel for gains from trade, and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) showed how the same logic separates exporting from foreign direct investment. The framework is more than twenty years old. It has been tested on firm-level administrative and customs data from many countries, which is the kind of register-based evidence I know best, and it is standard in teaching and in policy evaluation. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the case. The attribution objections concern parallel work that is not on this ballot entry, and none of them questions the originating role of Melitz or the extension and agenda-setting role of Helpman. I do not count the unanimity of opening proposals for the pair as merit. It only shows that the credit is easy to identify. The chair asks how to weigh breadth of influence against attribution cleanliness. B012 has the larger policy footprint, but its footprint is spread over strands that three names cannot separate without arbitrary exclusions. B026 has a somewhat narrower footprint but a defined discovery, a defined origin, and a record of repeated confirmation against micro data. When the two differ this much on attribution and are both mature, I let the attribution difference decide. This is a judgement about how defensible a citation is, not a claim that trade matters more than monetary policy. The part I now prefer to leave out is the two-part prize with B007. A combination of Kiyotaki and Moore with Melitz and Helpman would have four people, which exceeds the three-person cap. Melitz alone is the alternative, and I find a Melitz-only part harder to defend than a pair.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my configuration is that the credited set omits empirical and quantitative contributors. Bernard and Jensen established the exporter-premium facts that the theory explained, and Eaton and Kortum developed a parallel quantitative line. Only people on the ballot entry can be credited, and a citation that reads as honouring all of firm-level trade research would be an overreach. The citation therefore has to be worded around the theoretical framework. A second concern is overlap with the 2008 trade prize. I think the discoveries are distinct, but members such as Enflo and Teorell treat this as a live question, and I cannot settle it from the written record. A third concern is that welfare magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as the productivity distribution. The qualitative selection result is better established than the size of the gains. Finally, B012 has the most explicit first-choice support and a very large policy footprint. A committee that weights footprint above attribution would reasonably place it first.

responses.point: Boppart lists B026 as his second choice and accepts Melitz (2003) as the anchor. He argues that the Committee would have to explain why Helpman, rather than a contributor from the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line, is the second name. That is why he prefers B007, where the two-author credit has no obvious missing claimant.
responses.response: This is the most useful challenge to the second name, and I do not think it can be dismissed. My answer has two parts. First, the ballot entry limits the choice to Helpman, Melitz and Redding, so the question inside the entry is Helpman or Redding. Helpman's role runs through Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple and his wider heterogeneous-firm agenda, which makes him a co-developer of the framework itself. Redding's work builds on it. Second, Bernard and Jensen are chiefly the source of the empirical facts the framework explains, and Eaton and Kortum answer a different, Ricardian and quantitative question. Excluding them does not make the Melitz-Helpman citation false if it is worded around the theoretical framework. I agree that the pair leaves a real attribution cost. I read it as a limit on how widely the citation can be phrased, not as a reason to wait. Whether that cost is larger than the 2022-overlap cost for B007 is a judgement on which we differ.

responses.point: Krusell finds B026 a strong case and a close alternative, and would prefer it to his own part if the Committee decides that Melitz's originating role makes the pair sufficiently clear. He also notes that Helpman's credit is spread across the separate trade-politics entry.
responses.response: I take his conditional offer seriously, since it identifies exactly what the Committee needs to decide. On Helpman's credit being spread, I would argue the opposite. A laureate with several lines of work has more than one reason to be credited, but the citation names only the heterogeneous-firm contribution, so the other lines neither strengthen nor weaken this part. The question for the Committee is whether Melitz's originating role makes a Melitz-Helpman pair clear enough. I think it does, because the pair is the minimal set that covers both the originating model and its extension to firms' choice between exporting and foreign direct investment. I would add that his own earlier point about Kiyotaki and Moore applies in the same way here. Cleanliness of attribution is a reason to prefer a citation, not evidence that the discovery is larger.

responses.point: Strömberg proposes a two-part prize, Kiyotaki and Moore (B007) plus Melitz alone (B026). He says he would prefer to name Helpman but that the three-person cap prevents it, and he would support Melitz and Helpman if B026 stood alone.
responses.response: I appreciate that he identifies the cap as the source of the one-person part and not as a view on Helpman's claim. I would not support the combination as written. A Melitz-only citation leaves out the co-developer of the framework, and the Committee would have to explain that exclusion publicly. If the Committee wants to combine macro-finance and trade, the cap would force one of the two parts to be thinner than its attribution supports. I prefer one well-attributed part to two parts where one is distorted by the cap. His willingness to back Melitz and Helpman as a stand-alone part is, for me, the most relevant fact in that exchange. I note it as a reason B026 may be acceptable to colleagues whose first choice is B007, but I do not treat it as a vote count.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson, who ranks B026 first, wants the citation written around the heterogeneous-firm framework and not around all firm-level trade research. She would hold Redding back under the cap, but argues that adding him should be decided on the merits and not on the three-person limit.
responses.response: We agree on the wording, and the citation I propose follows that approach. I would keep Redding out for the reason I gave in round 1: his quantitative and spatial work builds on the framework and does not supply its central insight. I accept her condition that the exclusion must rest on the merits, not on the cap. If the Committee judged the quantitative-trade strand a separate discovery, the right response would be to treat it as such and not to add a third name to this part. I would also keep her point about the 2008 prize in view. Krugman's prize explained intra-industry trade and location with representative firms, and heterogeneous-firm selection is a later and empirically testable advance, but I cannot show this from the written record alone.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B012 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford because they are the most separable originators. He now treats B026 as a stronger alternative than he did at opening, and lists as remaining reservations the uncredited parallel contributors and Helpman's appearance under the trade-politics entry.
responses.response: I accept his separability argument for B012 and agree it is the best available way to cut that field. My difference with him is about how much arbitrariness remains after the cut. Even with three separable originators, the Committee must say publicly why Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler, who made the framework usable, are left out. I can state the corresponding omissions for B026 and they are narrower. They are parallel work outside the ballot entry, not contributors to the same framework. I also agree with his own reservation that the Taylor rule alone is a thin basis. This is why I keep B012 as a serious alternative and not as a weak one. On his reservation about Helpman's other entry, the citation names only the heterogeneous-firm contribution, so the other entry does not enter the credit.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would see the omission of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum as serious enough to make a Melitz-Helpman pair premature. I think not, but I cannot rule it out on the evidence I have.
Whether the heterogeneous-firm advance is distinct enough from the 2008 trade prize. I have argued it is, and I cannot show it from the written record alone.
How much of the gains-from-trade message depends on functional-form assumptions, as opposed to the more robust qualitative selection result.

Whether B012 should rank above B026 if breadth of policy influence is weighted more than attribution cleanliness. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or the empirical record beyond the supplied material.

I have moved B039 out of my alternatives. I have not resolved whether the technology-and-task work and the trade-shock work are one discovery or two, or which three of Autor, Hanson, Dorn and Katz would carry the credit. Until that is settled I cannot defend it as a final configuration.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for any candidate in my preferred part or alternatives. The profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Melitz, Helpman, Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Kiyotaki or Moore. My field of empirical labour and education economics is close to B039 and B018, which are not in my final configuration. I overlapped institutionally at Stockholm University (2010-17) with colleagues Hassler and Krusell, who are fellow members and not candidates. That overlap is not co-authorship. I disclose these connections without adjudicating them. My 2021 presentation speech and press-release statements as chair do not establish private preferences among the 2026 candidates.
